## Where the Framing Breaks Down

**This series reads an X-designation as a promise that something will be flown, and the X-54 breaks that reading in three places.**

**The first is that the aeroplane was never built.** Its question was posed by a registry entry and assigned a decade later to a different aeroplane under a different number, which at this article's date had not yet flown supersonically. **No record this article can reach explains why the X-54 was not built**, so the framing has no decision to examine.

**The second is that its question was regulatory, and the regulation moved without it.** The prohibition was ordered repealed by Executive Order 14304 on 6 June 2025 \[[Executive Order 14304, Leading the World in Supersonic Flight][ref_eo_14304]\]. The order specifies no technique \[[Executive Order 14304, Leading the World in Supersonic Flight][ref_eo_14304]\], and the article argues that the technique able to meet a noise-based rule without a new airframe is Mach cutoff rather than shaping. Signatures at cutoff Mach number were measured in flight and published in 1971 \[[Henderson et al. 1971][research_maglieri_cutoff]\]. The subsection headed The Alternative That Never Needed the Aeroplane sets out the argument. **An aeroplane justified by a rulemaking was overtaken by an older technique that needed no airframe.** Even the evidence a rulemaking consumes is human-response evidence, and the aeroplane would have supplied the stimulus for it rather than the evidence itself, as Thin Subjects records.

**The third is that the case for the aeroplane is narrower than the report that originated it.** The Quiet Spike report states that the aeroplane's own shocks would overtake the spike's within a short distance. With geometric spreading the coalescence does not complete at a strength difference of 0.01, so the case holds for a host the size of an F-15 only if its strength difference is 0.02 or more, which this article assumes, and the result cannot be extended to spikes in general. The calculation is in The Arithmetic the Report Set Out and Did Not Perform.

## The Source Base

**The eighty-six curated sources that carry the argument and the 2,357 that map the field are different things, and this article keeps them apart on purpose.**

**The evidentiary base is unusually documentary for an article about an aeroplane.** Eighty-six curated research records, seven books and thirty-two reference sources carry every claim made here, and the ones that matter most are a designation registry, an executive order, the final rule of 1973 and a flight test report that states in plain words why the experiment it describes could not produce the result its successor was designated to produce. **Those are not commentary on the evidence. They are the evidence.**

**The research survey maps the field, and none of it is cited in support of any claim about the X-54.** It holds 2,357 records in ten clusters, drawn from the Crossref scholarly registry, NASA's Technical Reports Server and the Defense Technical Information Center, of which 279 are report primaries, being 11.8 percent, by the identifier rule set out under The Definition of Primary. **There is nothing in it about the aeroplane, because the aeroplane was never built and no title in the survey names it.**

### The Age of the Literature Is Itself a Finding

**The literature of this subject has a shape, and the shape is the funding history.** 2,286 of the 2,357 research records carry a year in their reference anchor or in their entry in the References list, and their median is 2008. Every rate and share in this section is counted on that year, so the article's own source is enough to recount it.

**Publication ran at 25.3 records a year through the 1970s, fell to 13.9 through the 1980s, and has grown every decade since to 79.6 in the 2020s**, a decade whose count is divided by seven because the survey reaches seven years into it. The trough is 54.9 percent of the peak that preceded it, and the present rate is 5.7 times the trough. **The American supersonic transport was cancelled in 1971 and the prohibition took effect in 1973**, and the decade that follows those two dates is the only one in this corpus in which the yearly rate fell. Counted in records rather than records a year, the unfinished 2020s already hold 557 against 540 for the 2010s.

**The corpus is split almost evenly between the recent and the old.** 36.7 percent of the dated records were published in 2015 or later and 37.9 percent before 2000, which is a field with a long memory and an active present rather than either alone.

**The report primaries are older than the survey and their dates follow the agency's research programmes rather than the journals.** Of the 246 report primaries that carry a year, the median is 1992 against 2008 for the corpus, a gap of 16 years, and 84 date from before 1980. **The 1990s hold more of them than any other decade**, at 66. Of the 2,310 dated records published in 2000 or later, 74 are report primaries, so the recent literature is mostly journal and conference work. A report-primary fraction of 11.8 percent in a corpus whose median is 2008 is therefore reporting something about when the subject was funded.

### The Definition of Primary

**Primacy is a property of the document, and this survey derives it from the identifier.** A record is a report primary when its address is on the NASA Technical Reports Server or it carries a digital object identifier under the 10.21236 prefix, which Crossref registers for Defense Technical Information Center reports. **By that rule 279 of the 2,357 research records are report primaries, being 11.8 percent**, among them the Quiet Spike flight test report, the airborne data report of the shaped-boom demonstration, the cutoff measurements of 1971 and the cutoff investigation of 2012.

**The programmes' own bibliographies lead to the older documents, and those documents are cited directly.** The Quiet Spike flight test report, the shaped-boom demonstration paper and the cutoff investigation each name the documents they were built on. The curated references include the Gulfstream design chain from 2003 to 2009, the classical minimisation and propagation literature from 1956 to 1979, the human-response experiments the loudness procedure was calibrated against, and the standard atmosphere the article computes in.

**The measure sees most of this article's primary documents and misses the five that decide it.** A designation registry, an executive order, a final rule in the Federal Register, a part of the code of federal regulations and a patent carry no identifier the measure can read, and those five are what the argument turns on. **The rule does not reach the journal papers among the primary sources either**, such as Whitham on weak shocks and George and Seebass on minimisation, so 11.8 percent is a lower bound on how much of the survey is first-hand. **The count of named primary documents is reported beside the fraction rather than instead of it**, and the measure is not adjusted to flatter the number.

### Thin Subjects

**Six subjects that this article's derivations and conclusions depend on have thin literatures.** Each count below is the number of research records in this survey whose title carries at least one of the listed terms, with a hyphen read as a space. Where a row joins two groups of terms with the word together, a title must carry a term from each group.

| Subject | Title terms counted | Records |
|---|---|---|
| the X-54 itself | X-54, X-54A, X54 | 0 |
| the coalescence and aging of a signature | coalescence, coalescing, merging, overtaking, aging, ageing together with shock, shocks, boom, booms, signature, signatures, N-wave | 1 |
| the extendable nose spike | Quiet Spike, QuietSpike, extendable nose, telescoping nose | 17 |
| Mach cutoff flight | Mach cutoff, Mach cut-off, cutoff Mach, no-boom thresholds, threshold Mach number | 15 |
| the reflection of a boom at the ground | reflection factor, reflection factors, ground reflection, boom reflection, reflected sonic booms, reflected sonic boom | 4 |
| the overland prohibition | overland, over land, prohibition, 91.817 | 9 |

**No title names the X-54**, which is the fact the opening of this section states.

**The coalescence on which the case for the aeroplane rests is named in one title**, a study of the aging of sonic booms \[[Plotkin 1994][research_aging_of_booms]\], so the coalescence distances computed above rest on weak-shock theory rather than on a literature that measures them.

**The extendable nose spike is named in 17 titles, and 15 of them are the design, test and analysis reports of Gulfstream and the flight programme.** The other two, from 2019 and 2024, study the concept on a supersonic transport. **The spike's literature is its own programme's record**, which is why this article reads that record directly.

**Mach cutoff is named in 15 titles, and 2 of them date from 1971.** The other 13 date from 2015 or later, so for the 43 years from 1972 to 2014 no title in this survey names the technique that needs no new airframe to keep a boom off the ground.

**The reflection of a boom at the ground is named in 4 titles**, so the factor of about 1.9 that turns an incident wave into a measured one rests on the in-flight technique cited where the factor is derived rather than on a body of measurement.

**The overland prohibition is named in 9 titles, and one of them names the prohibition itself**, a reassessment of the merits of the FAA prohibition on civil supersonic flight published in 2018 \[[Petree 2018][research_petree_2018]\]. The rest concern overland flight itself, how it might be certified and what it would be worth.

**Fifty records of 2,357, or 2.1 percent, are about the rule.** That is the second smallest cluster in the survey, after the atmosphere. **The aeroplane's registry entry names a regulatory change process as its purpose, and the regulatory literature is the second thinnest shelf in a survey of its subject**, while 447 records, or 19.0 percent, are about what the noise does to the people who hear it. **The evidence a rulemaking actually consumes is human-response evidence**, and this article's aeroplane was designated to produce the stimulus for it.

**Two conclusions therefore rest on documents rather than on a literature.** The first is that a shaped nose on an otherwise ordinary aeroplane cannot deliver a shaped ground signature. It rests on a primary document rather than on the survey, being the flight test report of the programme that decided not to attempt it, and on an arithmetic that report did not perform. The second is that the rule is the deliverable and the aeroplane the evidence for it. It rests on the registry entry, which names a regulatory change process as the aeroplane's purpose, and on the executive order, and the regulatory shelf of the survey is its thinnest, at fifty records.

### What the Survey Admits

**A record is admitted only when a person reading its title finds that it bears on a subject this article's argument uses**, read against the article and not against a shared word. Those subjects are the sonic boom as a physical object and its minimisation, its propagation through the atmosphere and into water, the supersonic aerodynamics and configurations of the aircraft that make it, its computation and its measurement, the standard atmosphere, the response of people, buildings and animals to it, the other noise of aircraft, and the regulation and certification of aircraft noise. **No residual cluster is needed**, because every admitted title belongs to one of the ten named clusters.

Many words this subject depends on also name something else, and a record that shares only such a word is excluded. Impulsive noise also names an outlier in power-line, radio, image and speech data and in the algorithms of active noise control. Shadow zone and sound-speed profile also belong to ocean acoustics, sonar and marine seismic surveying, and shadow zone also to geotechnics and astrobiology. Near field and far field also belong to antenna and radar measurement, a supersonic jet is also a tool of laser spectroscopy and molecular beams, a boom is also a barrier for an oil spill and the tail of a helicopter, and Sonic Boom is also the title of a book about the music industry, an essay, an advertising study and a technique of ultrasound imaging. A tunnel sonic boom is the pressure wave a high-speed train radiates from a tunnel portal, a quiet tunnel is a low-disturbance wind tunnel, a standard atmosphere is also the conditioning climate for testing textiles and paper, and regulation also names a control law. Microphone arrays that listen for coughs, speech, gearbox faults or the modes of a structure are excluded for the same reason. **A record whose only link to this article is a distant application domain is excluded as well**, among them the internal flows of inlets, diffusers, nozzles and engines, which the article places out of scope, shock and boundary-layer interaction, combustion and aerodynamic heating, missile and projectile hardware, spikes and energy deposition ahead of blunt bodies where the title does not name the boom, laboratory shock physics, the subsystems and flight control of supersonic aircraft, planetary decelerators, gravity waves of the upper atmosphere, aircraft emissions and contrails, occupational and interior noise exposure and hearing protection, product sound quality, and laboratory studies of animal hearing. Correction, erratum, corrigendum, retraction and withdrawal notices are excluded as well, because a survey counts research works and a notice is an editorial event rather than a work. A review of a book, an unsigned news item, a reference or definition entry of two pages or fewer, a table of standard values of two pages or fewer printed as a textbook appendix, a journal's listing of a newly issued publication, the resolution of a standards conference and a second deposit of a document already in the survey, such as a report-server copy of a journal or conference paper, are not admitted either, while an authored encyclopedia article of more than two pages and a textbook chapter are research works and are kept.

**Some records of doubtful relevance are kept.** Community response to road, rail, wind turbine, industrial and other environmental noise, and general studies of annoyance, low-frequency noise and noise sensitivity, are kept because exposure-response methodology is one field and aircraft are one of its cases. The penetration of a sonic boom into water is kept as distinct from ocean acoustics, and so are the active control of a physical impulsive sound, laser beams distorted by an aircraft's shock, the drag of projectiles and missiles where the subject is wave drag, generic studies of shock propagation and acoustic ray tracing whose medium is not stated, and market and economic studies of supersonic aircraft and of aviation noise. Each shares the physics of the wave, its measurement or its human response with this subject, and a reader may weigh it accordingly.

**Every research title has been read for relevance, so the off-topic share that remains is a matter of reading judgement and not of sampling.** A reading of titles cannot show that a work is relevant in substance, so this is a statement about titles only.

## Epistemic State

**What is documentary fact.** The X-54A designation was allocated on 5 May 2008 to Gulfstream Aerospace with NASA as the sponsoring agency, with two Rolls-Royce Tay 651 engines and the mission statement quoted in full above. The Shaped Sonic Boom Demonstration flew on 27 August 2003 and measured a shaped signature on the ground. The Quiet Spike flew 32 flights on a NASA F-15B between August 2006 and February 2007, reached Mach 1.8 at 685 pounds per square foot, probed its near field at Mach 1.4, and did not attempt a ground measurement for the reason its report states. The prohibition on civil supersonic flight over the United States was published on 28 March 1973 and took effect on 27 April 1973, and Executive Order 14304 of 6 June 2025 directs its repeal within 180 days without naming any technique. The X-59 first flew on 28 October 2025, below the speed of sound.

**What is computed here and not taken from a source.** The coalescence distances both with and without geometric spreading, the ray path length, the cutoff Mach number and its temperature sensitivity, the turning altitude, the lateral cutoff azimuth, the Mach angles, the true airspeeds, the standard-atmosphere quantities, Concorde's cruise boom expressed as a level and as a pressure ratio, the consistency of 685 pounds per square foot with Mach 1.8 at 45,000 feet, and every count in the Source Base including the publication rates by decade.

**The coalescence calculation rests on an assumed range of shock-strength differences that no source in this article supplies**, and the article reports the range rather than a value for that reason. **It also depends on a reference distance at which that strength is quoted**, taken here as one aeroplane length, and both choices move the outcome. **The spreading-corrected result is the one to read**, and it does not support the conclusion at the weakest end of the range.

**What is secondary and marked as such.** The X-54's cruise Mach number, altitude and perceived-level target, and the account that the agency regarded the designation as a placeholder. **None of the argument depends on any of them.**

**What is cited from a document rather than through one.** The Gulfstream design chain, the classical minimisation and propagation papers, the human-response experiments and the standard atmosphere are all cited directly. **One source is absent.** The standard monograph of this subject is named by the cutoff investigation's bibliography, and its report-server identifier is not verifiable, so it is not cited here.

**What is an approximation rather than a result.** The spreading correction assumes both shocks weaken as the inverse square root of distance and that they weaken proportionally, neither of which is exact once the wave begins to age. **It is a bound rather than a prediction**, and a propagation code of the kind the discipline actually uses would answer the question properly \[[Lonzaga et al. 2025][research_pcboom_technical]\]. The Mach cutoff relation likewise assumes a horizontally stratified atmosphere and still air, and the article states the wind term without using it.

**What is not known.** Why the aeroplane was not built. No primary document reviewed here records a decision, and the absence of a cancellation record is not evidence of a cancellation. **Also unknown is whether the interim standard the executive order directs was in place on the deadline**, which falls four days after this article's date and therefore outside what it can report.

**What this article does not claim.** It does not claim that low-boom shaping is unnecessary, and the shaping literature is the fifth largest cluster in the article's survey for good reason. **It claims that the regulatory change the X-54 was designated to support was ordered before the evidence it was designated to produce existed**, by an order silent on technique, and that a demonstrator justified by a rulemaking is exposed to the rulemaking moving without it. **That Mach cutoff is the technique able to meet a noise-based rule without a new airframe is this article's inference** from the cutoff relation and the 1971 and 2012 measurements, and the order does not say so.

## Out of Scope

**The economics of supersonic business travel.** Whether a market exists for an aeroplane of this kind is the question that decided whether anybody would pay for it, and this article makes no claim about it.

**The landing and take-off noise of a supersonic aeroplane**, which is a separate regulatory track with a standard, a metric and a literature of its own. The survey above reports that cluster as part of the field it maps, and the article does not argue from it.

**The propulsion.** Two Rolls-Royce Tay 651 engines are what the registry records, and what a low-boom airframe demands of an inlet and a nozzle is a large subject this article touches only where the equivalent area distribution requires it.

**Everything after this article's date.** The executive order sets a deadline four days ahead of it, and what the agency did on that deadline is not something this article can report.

## Conclusion

**An X-designation is usually a promise that something will be flown, and this series has already documented several that were not.**

The X-54A's registry entry made a narrower promise than most. It promised ground sonic boom signatures, in support of a regulatory change process, and it made that promise in 2008 because a flight test programme had established, in a report published the year before, that no existing aeroplane could produce them. **The gap was real and the entry names it precisely.**

**The argument for filling it survives arithmetic, though not quite in the form the report states it.** Working the overtaking through weak-shock theory shows that the spike's shocklets are consumed before the ground, about halfway down the ray path at the weakest, at the strength differences this article assumes for an aeroplane the size of the one they were bolted to, and that the same calculation would come out differently on a weaker or longer host. **The programme's reason was right about its own aeroplane, though not about spikes in general**, a smaller claim than the report makes and a sufficient one for what followed.

**Nothing was built.** The evidence the entry describes is assigned to a different aeroplane under a different number a decade later, which had not flown supersonically by this article's date, and in the meantime the prohibition was ordered repealed by an order that leaves the technique open, while a technique that makes no ground boom at all, rather than a quiet one, needed no new airframe to meet the noise-based rule the order calls for.

**That technique is not new and this article's most surprising finding is how old it is.** Signatures at cutoff Mach number were measured in flight and published in 1971, 2 years before the prohibition took effect and 54 years before the order to repeal it \[[Henderson et al. 1971][research_maglieri_cutoff]\]. **The aeroplane was overtaken not by a newer idea but by an older one**, which had been sitting in the same agency's report server throughout and needed no airframe to make its case.

**The lesson is not that the aeroplane was unnecessary.** The X-59 exists, which is the strongest possible argument that somebody still needs what the X-54 was for. **The lesson is that an aeroplane whose justification is a rulemaking has tied itself to a clock it does not control**, and this one was overtaken by its own regulation in much the way its predecessor's shocklets were overtaken by the aeroplane carrying them.

**The number was allocated 17.6 years before the date on this article. The rule is being repealed, its replacement flew last month, and X-54A has still never been built.**

## Equations

<!-- Equations generated by _lib/equations.py from _sources/equations/. Edit the data file and regenerate. Do not edit this section by hand. -->

This section collects the 31 display equations of the article in the order they appear,
each under its number and reproduced exactly as it stands in the text.
A title in bold names an established result,
and a title in italics beginning with the word Bespoke names a construction made for this analysis.
Of the 31, 30 are established and 1 are bespoke.
Atmospheric relations are in units of the International System, with altitudes in metres, temperatures in kelvin and pressures in pascals, while overpressures and dynamic pressures quoted from flight reports are in pounds per square foot and levels are in decibels referred to 20 micropascals, and several letters are kept apart deliberately, so $T$ is the temperature and $T_{N}$ the N-wave duration, $L$ is the lapse rate and $\mathcal{L}$ the coalescence distance, $R$ is the gas constant and $\mathcal{R}$ the ground reflection coefficient.

**Equation 1, Mach Angle.**
The disturbances of a supersonic body lie on a cone whose half-angle has a sine equal to the reciprocal of the Mach number.
[Mach Number][ref_mach_number]
[Liepmann and Roshko, Elements of gasdynamics][book_liepmann_roshko]

$$
\mu \;=\; \arcsin\!\left(\frac{1}{M}\right),
\tag{1}
$$

**Equation 2, Speed of Sound in a Perfect Gas.**
The speed of sound in a perfect gas is the square root of the ratio of specific heats times the gas constant times the absolute temperature.
[Anderson, Modern compressible flow][book_anderson_compressible]

$$
a \;=\; \sqrt{\gamma R T}.
\tag{2}
$$

**Equation 3, Straight Ray Path From Cruise Altitude to the Ground.**
A ray leaving normal to the Mach cone makes the Mach angle with the vertical, so its straight path to the ground is the altitude divided by the cosine of that angle.
[Haefeli et al. 1969a][research_hayes_cr1299]

$$
r \;=\; \frac{h}{\cos\mu} \;=\; \frac{h}{\sqrt{1 - M^{-2}}}.
\tag{3}
$$

**Equation 4, Propagation Speed of a Weak Shock.**
A weak shock outruns the speed of sound by a fraction proportional to its strength, with coefficient the ratio of one more than the ratio of specific heats to four times that ratio.
[Whitham, Linear and nonlinear waves][book_whitham]
[Hamilton and Blackstock, Nonlinear acoustics][book_hamilton_blackstock]

$$
\frac{U}{a} \;=\; 1 \;+\; \frac{\gamma+1}{4\gamma}\,\frac{\Delta p}{p} \;+\; \mathcal{O}\!\left(\frac{\Delta p}{p}\right)^{2}.
\tag{4}
$$

**Equation 5, Linear Pressure Profile of an N-Wave.**
The N-wave is a linear fall in overpressure from its peak to its negative peak between two jumps over the duration $T_{N}$.
[Darden 1976][research_darden_1976]
[Application of sonic-boom minimization concepts in supersonic transport design][research_carlson_sst_design]

$$
\Delta p(t) \;=\; \Delta p_{\max}\left(1 - \frac{2t}{T_{N}}\right), \qquad 0 \le t \le T_{N},
\tag{5}
$$

**Equation 6, Positive-Phase Impulse of an N-Wave.**
Integrating the overpressure over the positive half of the N-wave gives an impulse of one quarter of the peak overpressure times the duration $T_{N}$.
[McCurdy 1994][research_boom_shapes_risetimes]

$$
I \;=\; \int_{0}^{T_{N}/2}\Delta p(t)\,\mathrm{d}t \;=\; \frac{\Delta p_{\max} T_{N}}{4}.
\tag{6}
$$

**Equation 7, Whitham F-Function.**
Whitham's F-function gives the far-field disturbance of a slender supersonic body as an Abel-type integral of the second derivative of its equivalent area distribution.
[Whitham 1952][research_whitham_1952]
[Ashley and Landahl, Aerodynamics of wings and bodies][book_ashley_landahl]

$$
F(y) \;=\; \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{y} \frac{A_e''(\xi)}{\sqrt{y-\xi}}\;\mathrm{d}\xi .
\tag{7}
$$

**Equation 8, Equivalent Area Including Lift.**
The equivalent area adds to the physical cross-section a term proportional to the lift carried ahead of each station, so a lifting surface displaces the air whether or not it is thick.
[Darden 1976][research_darden_1976]

$$
A_e(x) \;=\; A(x) \;+\; \frac{\beta}{2q}\int_{0}^{x} \ell(\xi)\,\mathrm{d}\xi ,
\qquad \beta = \sqrt{M^{2}-1}.
\tag{8}
$$

**Equation 9, Lift Contribution to the Equivalent Area at the Tail.**
By the tail all of the lift has entered the equivalent area, contributing $\beta W / 2q$ whatever the shaping.

$$
A_{L}(l) \;=\; \frac{\beta W}{2q},
\tag{9}
$$

**Equation 10, Square-Root Dependence of Overpressure on Weight.**
A fully aged N-wave amplitude goes as the square root of the F-function amplitude, which is linear in the lift, so overpressure scales as the square root of weight.
[McLean 1965][research_mclean_nonasymptotic]
[Application of sonic-boom minimization concepts in supersonic transport design][research_carlson_sst_design]

$$
\Delta p \;\propto\; W^{1/2}.
\tag{10}
$$

**Equation 11, Near-Field Overpressure From the F-Function.**
Before nonlinear steepening, the overpressure ratio is proportional to the F-function and falls as the inverse square root of distance.
[On the propagation of weak shock waves][research_whitham_1956]

$$
\frac{\Delta p}{p_\infty} \;=\; \frac{\gamma M^{2}}{\sqrt{2\beta}}\,\frac{F(y)}{\sqrt{r}} ,
\tag{11}
$$

**Equation 12, Far-Field Decay of N-Wave Amplitude and Duration.**
Once aged into an N-wave, the overpressure falls as the minus three-quarters power of distance and the duration grows as its one-quarter power.
[On the propagation of weak shock waves][research_whitham_1956]
[Haefeli et al. 1969a][research_hayes_cr1299]

$$
\Delta p \;\propto\; r^{-3/4}, \qquad \Delta t \;\propto\; r^{1/4}.
\tag{12}
$$

**Equation 13, Slender-Body Wave Drag Functional.**
In linearised supersonic flow the wave drag of a slender body is a double integral of the second derivative of the same equivalent area distribution with a logarithmic kernel.
[Ashley and Landahl, Aerodynamics of wings and bodies][book_ashley_landahl]

$$
D \;=\; -\frac{q}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{l}\!\!\int_{0}^{l} A_e''(x_{1})\,A_e''(x_{2})\,
\ln\lvert x_{1}-x_{2}\rvert \;\mathrm{d}x_{1}\,\mathrm{d}x_{2}.
\tag{13}
$$

**Equation 14, Troposphere of the Standard Atmosphere.**
Below the tropopause the temperature falls linearly with altitude and hydrostatic equilibrium in a perfect gas makes the pressure a power of the temperature ratio.
[U.S. Standard Atmosphere][ref_us_standard_atmosphere]

$$
T(z) \;=\; T_{0} - Lz, \qquad
p(z) \;=\; p_{0}\left(\frac{T(z)}{T_{0}}\right)^{g/LR},
\tag{14}
$$

**Equation 15, Isothermal Layer of the Standard Atmosphere.**
Above the tropopause the temperature is constant and the pressure falls exponentially with altitude.
[U.S. Standard Atmosphere 1976 1976][research_us_standard_atmosphere_1976]

$$
p(z) \;=\; p_{11}\exp\!\left[-\frac{g\,(z - z_{11})}{R\,T_{11}}\right].
\tag{15}
$$

**Equation 16, Dynamic Pressure in Terms of Static Pressure and Mach Number.**
The dynamic pressure of a perfect gas is half the ratio of specific heats times the static pressure times the square of the Mach number.
[Liepmann and Roshko, Elements of gasdynamics][book_liepmann_roshko]

$$
q \;=\; \tfrac{1}{2}\rho V^{2} \;=\; \frac{\gamma}{2}\,p\,M^{2}.
\tag{16}
$$

**Equation 17, Excess Propagation Speed of a Weak Shock.**
The speed by which a weak shock exceeds the speed of sound is the speed of sound times the strength coefficient times the pressure ratio.
[On the propagation of weak shock waves][research_whitham_1956]

$$
\Delta U \;=\; a\,\frac{\gamma+1}{4\gamma}\,\frac{\Delta p}{p},
\tag{17}
$$

**Equation 18, Coalescence Distance of Two Shocks.**
Two shocks a distance $s$ apart merge after a travel distance equal to $s$ divided by the difference in their excess speeds, in which the speed of sound cancels.
[On the propagation of weak shock waves][research_whitham_1956]

$$
\mathcal{L} \;=\; \frac{a\,s}{\Delta U_{1}-\Delta U_{2}} \;=\; s\,\frac{4\gamma}{(\gamma+1)}\left[\frac{\Delta p_{1}-\Delta p_{2}}{p}\right]^{-1}.
\tag{18}
$$

**Equation 19, Aging Length of a Weak Wave.**
The aging length of nonlinear acoustics is the distance over which a wave of length $s$ and relative strength $\Delta p / p$ distorts into its asymptotic form.
[Whitham, Linear and nonlinear waves][book_whitham]
[Hamilton and Blackstock, Nonlinear acoustics][book_hamilton_blackstock]

$$
r_{\text{age}} \;\sim\; s\,\frac{4\gamma}{(\gamma+1)}\,\frac{p}{\Delta p}.
\tag{19}
$$

*Equation 20, Bespoke Coalescence Distance With Cylindrical Spreading.*
The article lets the strength difference between the two shocks decay as the inverse square root of distance from a reference distance it takes as one aeroplane length, and integrates the separation to zero.
[Darden et al. 1989][research_boom_methodology_status]

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}s}{\mathrm{d}r} \;=\; -\frac{\gamma+1}{4\gamma}\,\delta_{0}\sqrt{\frac{r_{0}}{r}}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\sqrt{r_{c}} \;=\; \sqrt{r_{0}} \;+\; \frac{\mathcal{L}}{2\sqrt{r_{0}}},
\tag{20}
$$

**Equation 21, Ray Invariant in a Stratified Atmosphere.**
In a horizontally stratified medium the local speed of sound divided by the cosine of the ray angle below the horizontal is conserved along a ray as the trace velocity.
[Pierce, Acoustics, an introduction to its physical principles and applications][book_pierce]

$$
\frac{a(z)}{\cos\theta(z)} \;=\; V_{t} \;=\; \text{constant},
\tag{21}
$$

**Equation 22, Hyperbolic Tangent Shock Profile.**
A steady balance between nonlinear steepening and diffusion gives a shock front with a hyperbolic tangent profile of characteristic time $\tau$.
[Blackstock, Fundamentals of physical acoustics][book_blackstock]

$$
\Delta p(t) \;=\; \frac{\Delta p_{\max}}{2}\left[1 - \tanh\!\left(\frac{t}{\tau}\right)\right],
\tag{22}
$$

**Equation 23, Inverse Dependence of Shock Thickness on Amplitude.**
The rise time of the steady shock varies inversely with its amplitude, so a weaker boom also rises more slowly.
[Blackstock, Fundamentals of physical acoustics][book_blackstock]

$$
\tau \;\propto\; \frac{1}{\Delta p}.
\tag{23}
$$

**Equation 24, Sound Pressure Level.**
An overpressure becomes a level as twenty times the base-ten logarithm of its ratio to the reference pressure of 20 micropascals.
[A loudness calculation procedure applied to shaped sonic booms][research_loudness_procedure]

$$
L_{p} \;=\; 20\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{\Delta p}{p_{\mathrm{ref}}}\right),
\qquad p_{\mathrm{ref}} = 20\ \mu\mathrm{Pa},
\tag{24}
$$

**Equation 25, Concorde Overpressure as a Fraction of Ambient Pressure.**
The measured Concorde overpressure of 1.94 pounds per square foot at Mach 2 and 52,000 feet is about one part in 1,090 of the ambient pressure.
[NASA Facts FS-2003-11-016, Sonic Booms][ref_nasa_sonic_booms]

$$
\frac{\Delta p}{p_{\infty}} \;=\; 9.17 \times 10^{-4},
\tag{25}
$$

**Equation 26, Ground Reflection of the Incident Wave.**
A gauge on a hard surface reads the incident wave plus its reflection, about 1.9 times the incident overpressure for a reflection coefficient near 0.9.
[Stansbery et al. 1999][research_midfield_signatures]

$$
\Delta p_{\text{measured}} \;=\; (1 + \mathcal{R})\,\Delta p_{\text{incident}}
\;\approx\; 1.9\,\Delta p_{\text{incident}},
\qquad \mathcal{R} \approx 0.9,
\tag{26}
$$

**Equation 27, Sound Exposure Level.**
The sound exposure level is ten times the base-ten logarithm of the time integral of the squared pressure ratio, referred to one second.

$$
\mathrm{SEL} \;=\; 10\log_{10}\!\left[\frac{1}{t_{\mathrm{ref}}}\int \frac{p^{2}(t)}{p_{\mathrm{ref}}^{2}}\,\mathrm{d}t\right],
\qquad t_{\mathrm{ref}} = 1\ \mathrm{s}.
\tag{27}
$$

**Equation 28, Mach Cutoff Number in Still Air.**
A boom fails to reach the ground when the shock's ground intersection is slower than sound at the surface, so the cutoff Mach number is the square root of the ratio of ground to cruise temperature.
[U.S. Standard Atmosphere][ref_us_standard_atmosphere]
[Anderson, Modern compressible flow][book_anderson_compressible]

$$
M_{\mathrm{co}} \;=\; \frac{a_{\text{ground}}}{a_{\text{cruise}}} \;=\; \sqrt{\frac{T_{\text{ground}}}{T_{\text{cruise}}}}.
\tag{28}
$$

**Equation 29, Turning Altitude in the Standard Troposphere.**
Setting the linear tropospheric speed of sound equal to the trace velocity gives a turning altitude linear in the square of the Mach number.
[Coulouvrat 2002][research_coulouvrat_shadow]

$$
z_{\text{turn}} \;=\; \frac{T_{0} - M^{2}\,T_{\text{cruise}}}{L}.
\tag{29}
$$

**Equation 30, Effective Sound Speed and Cutoff Mach Number With Wind.**
Wind adds its component along the ray to the thermodynamic speed of sound, so the cutoff Mach number is the ratio of the effective ground sound speed to the sound speed at cruise altitude.
[Haefeli et al. 1969a][research_hayes_cr1299]

$$
c_{\mathrm{eff}}(z) \;=\; a(z) + \mathbf{u}(z)\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}},
\qquad
M_{\mathrm{co}} \;=\; \frac{c_{\mathrm{eff}}(0)}{a(z_{\text{cruise}})} .
\tag{30}
$$

**Equation 31, Lateral Extent of the Boom Carpet.**
A ray leaving at azimuth $\phi$ reaches the ground only while the Mach number times the cosine of the azimuth exceeds the cutoff Mach number, which bounds the half-width of the carpet.
[Cliatt et al. 2016a][research_faint_lateral_cutoff]

$$
M\cos\phi \;\ge\; M_{\mathrm{co}}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\phi_{\max} \;=\; \arccos\!\left(\frac{M_{\mathrm{co}}}{M}\right).
\tag{31}
$$

### Notation

- $\mu$, the Mach angle
- $M$, the flight Mach number
- $a$, the speed of sound
- $\gamma$, the ratio of specific heats, taken as 1.4 for air
- $R$, the specific gas constant of air
- $h$, the cruise altitude
- $U$, the propagation speed of a weak shock
- $\Delta p$, the overpressure, with $\Delta p_{\max}$ its peak
- $p_\infty$, the ambient pressure at cruise altitude
- $T_{N}$, the duration of the N-wave
- $F(y)$, Whitham's F-function
- $A_e$, the equivalent area distribution, with $A$ the geometric cross-section
- $\ell$, the lift per unit length
- $\beta$, the Prandtl-Glauert factor $\sqrt{M^{2}-1}$
- $A_{L}$, the lift contribution to the equivalent area at the tail
- $W$, the aircraft weight
- $q$, the dynamic pressure
- $D$, the wave drag
- $L$, the temperature lapse rate of the troposphere
- $T_{11}$, the temperature of the isothermal layer, with $p_{11}$ and $z_{11}$ the pressure and altitude at its base
- $\mathcal{L}$, the coalescence distance of two shocks
- $r_{\text{age}}$, the aging length
- $\delta_{0}$, the strength difference between two shocks at the reference distance $r_{0}$
- $r_{c}$, the coalescence distance corrected for spreading
- $V_{t}$, the horizontal trace velocity of the wavefront
- $\theta$, the ray angle below the horizontal
- $\tau$, the characteristic rise time of the shock
- $L_{p}$, the sound pressure level
- $p_{\mathrm{ref}}$, the reference pressure of 20 micropascals
- $\mathcal{R}$, the ground reflection coefficient
- $\mathrm{SEL}$, the sound exposure level
- $M_{\mathrm{co}}$, the cutoff Mach number
- $z_{\text{turn}}$, the altitude at which a ray turns horizontal
- $c_{\mathrm{eff}}$, the effective sound speed including the wind component along the ray
- $\phi$, the azimuth of a ray from the ground track
